questions.stemHtml: Identify the following intracytoplasmic inclusion isolated from brain biopsy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Negri bodies

 

The image depicts Negri bodies, which are characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies seen in neurons infected with the rabies virus. These eosinophilic (pink-colored) inclusions are found in the cytoplasm of neurons, particularly in the hippocampus and cerebellum of the brain. Rabies, caused by the rabies virus (a member of the Rhabdoviridae family), is known for its affinity for neural tissues. Negri bodies are formed during viral replication within the cytoplasm of the neuron.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Paschen bodies: Incorrect because Paschen bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies associated with variola virus (smallpox). They are not found in brain biopsies but rather in infected epithelial cells.

 

Option C. Molluscum bodies: Incorrect because Molluscum bodies (also known as Henderson-Peterson bodies) are intracytoplasmic inclusions associated with Molluscum contagiosum, a poxvirus infection of the skin, not the brain.

 

Option D. Guarnieri bodies: Incorrect because Guarnieri bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions seen in infections with vaccinia virus or other poxviruses. They are also not found in neural tissue.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Negri bodies are diagnostic of rabies and are eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies found in neurons, particularly in the hippocampus and cerebellum.

 

Additional Information: 

 

Types of Inclusion Bodies

 

Inclusion bodies can be categorized based on their location within the host cell, as mentioned in the transcript:

 

1. Intracytoplasmic Inclusion Bodies:

 

  • Found in the cytoplasm of host cells.
  • Examples:
    • Negri bodies (Rabies virus)
    • Guarnieri bodies (Vaccinia virus)
    • Paschen bodies (Variola virus)
    • Bollinger bodies (Fowlpox virus)
    • Henderson-Peterson bodies (Molluscum contagiosum)

 

2. Intranuclear Inclusion Bodies:

 

  • Found in the nucleus of host cells.
  • Two types:
    • Cowdry Type A: Granular appearance (e.g., Herpesvirus, Varicella-Zoster virus, Yellow fever virus).

 

 

  • Cowdry Type B: Compact, circumscribed appearance (e.g., Polio, Adenovirus).

 

 

3. Inclusions in Both Cytoplasm and Nucleus:

 

  • Found in both the cytoplasm and nucleus of host cells.
  • Examples:
    • Measles virus (Warthin-Finkeldey bodies)
    • Cytomegalovirus (Owl-eye appearance)

questions.stem: A child presented with umbilicated pearly lesions in the face following this; mother also had developed the same lesion. Identify the virus causing a lesion?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pox virus

 

The described clinical scenario is characteristic of molluscum contagiosum, which is caused by a member of the poxvirus family. Molluscum contagiosum presents as umbilicated pearly lesions with a central depression, typically found on the face, trunk, or extremities. The disease is highly contagious and can spread from child to caregiver, as indicated in this case.

 

Key distinguishing features:

 

  • Umbilicated lesions: These lesions have a central depression or dimple, a hallmark of molluscum contagiosum.

 

 

  • Highly communicable: Transmission occurs via direct contact or fomites.
  • Virus family: Molluscum contagiosum belongs to the poxvirus family, which includes other members such as variola (smallpox) and vaccinia.

 

Other Options

 

Option B. HPV (Human Papillomavirus): Incorrect because HPV causes warts, which are raised, rough lesions without a central depression. HPV does not produce umbilicated lesions.

 

Option C. Varicella-zoster virus: Incorrect because Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox (vesicular lesions that evolve to crusts) and shingles (painful vesicular eruptions along a dermatomal distribution). Neither presents as umbilicated lesions.

 

Option D. Herpes simplex virus: Incorrect because Herpes simplex virus causes grouped vesicular lesions on an erythematous base, which are painful and do not have the characteristic umbilication seen in molluscum contagiosum.

 

Additional Information: Non-Cultivable Nature of Molluscum Contagiosum

 

  • Molluscum contagiosum is unique as it cannot be cultivated using standard laboratory techniques, such as tissue culture, embryonated eggs, or animal models. This is an important exception among viruses.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Umbilicated pearly lesions, particularly in children and close contacts, are diagnostic of molluscum contagiosum, caused by a member of the poxvirus family.

questions.stem: Guarnieri inclusion body is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Vaccinia

 

Guarnieri bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies seen in cells infected with the vaccinia virus, a member of the poxvirus family. These inclusion bodies are formed as a result of viral replication and assembly in the cytoplasm of host cells.

 

Key distinguishing features:

 

  • Intracytoplasmic inclusion: Guarnieri bodies are specific to vaccinia virus and are not found in other poxviruses like variola or molluscum contagiosum.
  • Artificial virus: Vaccinia is a modified form of variola virus, used in the preparation of the smallpox vaccine.
  • Historical significance: Smallpox, caused by variola virus, was eradicated in 1980, and the smallpox vaccine (made using vaccinia virus) is no longer in routine use.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fowl pox: Incorrect because Fowlpox virus produces Bollinger bodies, not Guarnieri bodies.

 

Option B. HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus): Incorrect because HSV forms intranuclear inclusions, such as Cowdry Type A bodies, and not intracytoplasmic inclusions like Guarnieri bodies.

 

Option C. Molluscum contagiosum: Incorrect because Molluscum contagiosum forms intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies called Henderson-Peterson bodies, not Guarnieri bodies.

 

Additional Information

 

  • Variola vs. Vaccinia: Variola, the virus responsible for smallpox, forms Paschen bodies, while vaccinia forms Guarnieri bodies. Although related, vaccinia is an artificial virus developed from variola for vaccine preparation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Guarnieri inclusion bodies are diagnostic of vaccinia virus infection and were historically significant in the development of the smallpox vaccine.

questions.stem: All are about polio, except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 90% paralytic  

 

Polio is caused by the poliovirus, a member of the Picornaviridae family. Most poliovirus infections are asymptomatic or present with minor illness. Paralytic polio is rare, occurring in less than 1% of cases.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 99% nonparalytic: Correct. The vast majority of polio cases are nonparalytic, either asymptomatic or presenting with mild symptoms.

 

Option B. Flaccid paralysis: Correct. Paralytic polio leads to asymmetric flaccid paralysis, also known as acute flaccid paralysis (AFP), affecting motor neurons.

 

Option C. Aseptic meningitis: Correct. A small percentage of patients develop nonparalytic aseptic meningitis with symptoms such as neck stiffness and back pain.

 

 

Additional Information:

 

Clinical Presentations of Polio:

 

  1. Inapparent (95%): No symptoms but detectable virus in stool or antibodies in the blood.
  2. Abortive Polio (4%): Mild, self-limiting flu-like illness.
  3. Nonparalytic Polio (<1%): Presents with aseptic meningitis.
  4. Paralytic Polio (<1%): Acute flaccid paralysis with no sensory loss.

 

Paralysis in Polio:

 

  • Asymmetric: Proximal muscles are more affected than distal.
  • Flaccid: Results in atrophy of the affected muscles.
  • Descending: Begins in the proximal muscles and progresses downward.
  • No sensory loss: Only motor neurons are affected.
  • Respiratory failure: If respiratory muscles are affected, it may lead to death.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Paralytic polio occurs in less than 1% of cases, with the majority being nonparalytic or asymptomatic. Paralytic polio is characterized by asymmetric flaccid paralysis without sensory loss.

questions.stem: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) JC virus 

 

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a rare, demyelinating disease of the central nervous system caused by JC virus. JC virus is a member of the Polyomaviridae family and primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with AIDS or transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy.

 

Key features of JC virus and PML:

 

  1. Virus family: JC virus belongs to the Polyomavirus group within the Papovaviridae family (Pe-Po-Va: Papilloma, Polyoma, and Vacuolating viruses).
  2. Host susceptibility: JC virus remains latent in the kidneys and lymphoid tissue of most people and is typically reactivated in immunocompromised states.
  3. Clinical features of PML:
    • Progressive neurological deficits such as cognitive impairment, motor weakness, and visual disturbances.
    • Caused by demyelination of white matter in multiple regions of the brain.
  4. High-risk groups: AIDS patients and transplant recipients are most vulnerable.

 

Note:

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. CMV (Cytomegalovirus): Incorrect because CMV causes retinitis, esophagitis, and systemic infections in immunocompromised individuals but does not cause PML.

 

Option B. EBV (Epstein-Barr Virus): Incorrect because EBV is associated with infectious mononucleosis, Burkitt lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Although it can cause CNS complications, it is not responsible for PML.

 

Option D. RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus): Incorrect because RSV is a respiratory virus that primarily causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia in children, not neurological disorders like PML.

 

Additional Information

 

  • JC virus-related diseases: In addition to PML, JC virus can rarely cause other CNS diseases such as JC virus granule cell neuronopathy.
  • Differential diagnosis of PML: Other causes of white matter demyelination in immunocompromised patients include HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) and CNS lymphoma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a demyelinating disease caused by the JC virus, a Polyomavirus that primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, including AIDS and transplant patients.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has undergone lung transplantation. Two months after transplantation, he developed pulmonary symptoms and diagnosed as having bilateral diffuse interstitial pulmonary pneumonitis and bronchiolitis. Which of the following etiological agent is responsible in this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cytomegalovirus 

 

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common cause of viral infections in immunocompromised individuals, including post-transplant and AIDS patients. After lung transplantation, the patient is on lifelong immunosuppressive therapy, which predisposes them to opportunistic infections. CMV often causes diffuse interstitial pneumonia, a hallmark clinical manifestation in transplant recipients.

 

Key points about CMV in immunocompromised states:

 

  1. Timing post-transplant: CMV infections typically occur 1 to 4 months after transplantation, consistent with this case.
  2. Clinical presentation:
    • Pulmonary symptoms: CMV pneumonitis presents as bilateral diffuse interstitial pneumonia.
    • May progress to bronchiolitis.
  3. Diagnosis: Characteristic owl-eye inclusion bodies are seen on histopathology of infected cells, indicating CMV infection.
  4. Other manifestations in immunocompromised patients:
    • In AIDS patients (CD4 count <50), CMV commonly causes retinitis, colitis, and esophagitis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV): Incorrect because HSV typically causes localized infections, such as herpes labialis or genital herpes, and rarely presents as diffuse pneumonia in immunocompromised patients.

 

Option C. Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV): Incorrect because EBV is associated with infectious mononucleosis, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and B-cell malignancies (e.g., Burkitt lymphoma) but does not cause interstitial pneumonia in transplant patients.

 

Option D. Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV): Incorrect because VZV typically causes chickenpox or shingles. While it may lead to pneumonia, this is rare and more common in immunocompromised patients during active VZV reactivation, not in the timeframe provided.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cytomegalovirus is the most common viral cause of interstitial pneumonia in transplant recipients, typically occurring 1 to 4 months post-transplant and characterized by owl-eye inclusion bodies on histology.

questions.stem: Space vehicle virus is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Adenovirus 

 

Adenovirus is nicknamed the "space vehicle virus" due to its unique structure that resembles a space vehicle. This appearance is due to the capsid's symmetrical arrangement of hexons and pentons, along with the knob-like projections.

 

 

Key features of adenovirus structure:

 

  1. Capsid: The protein coat surrounding the viral DNA core is composed of 252 capsomers:
    • 240 hexons: Form the main structure of the capsid (blue regions in diagrams).
    • 12 pentons: Located at the vertices, with each penton attached to a knob-like projection, creating the "space vehicle" appearance.
  2. Nucleic acid: Adenovirus contains double-stranded DNA at its core.
  3. Infectivity: Adenoviruses cause various infections, including respiratory diseases, conjunctivitis (pink eye), gastroenteritis, and hemorrhagic cystitis.

 

The space vehicle-like morphology is a distinctive feature, often tested in examinations.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reovirus: Incorrect because reovirus is a double-stranded RNA virus with a spherical, non-enveloped capsid, and does not resemble a space vehicle.

 

Option B. Rhabdovirus: Incorrect because rhabdovirus, which includes rabies virus, is bullet-shaped and does not exhibit the space vehicle-like structure.

 

Option C. Retrovirus: Incorrect because retrovirus, including HIV, has a spherical, enveloped capsid and does not have the structural features resembling a space vehicle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Adenovirus, a double-stranded DNA virus with a capsid composed of 252 capsomers, is called the "space vehicle virus" due to its unique structure.

questions.stem: Lysogenic conversion is:

options.label: A
options.text: New properties in a bacterium due to integration of phage genome

options.label: B
options.text: Transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another by bacteriophage

options.label: D
options.text: Transfer of genome during physical contact

questions.answerText: New properties in a bacterium due to integration of phage genome
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) New properties in a bacterium due to integration of phage genome

 

Lysogenic conversion occurs when a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) integrates its genome into the host bacterium's DNA. The bacteriophage genome becomes part of the bacterial genome without causing the immediate death of the host. This process can introduce new genetic traits to the bacterium, such as toxin production or antibiotic resistance, enhancing the bacterium's virulence or adaptability.

 

Key points about lysogenic conversion:

 

  • Integration of phage genome: The bacteriophage DNA integrates with the bacterial DNA, forming a prophage.

 

 

  • New traits: The bacterium gains new properties, such as toxin production (e.g., diphtheria toxin in Corynebacterium diphtheriae).
  • Temperate cycle: Unlike the lytic cycle, the lysogenic cycle does not kill the host bacterium.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another by bacteriophage: Incorrect because this describes transduction, not lysogenic conversion. Transduction involves the transfer of bacterial DNA between bacteria by a bacteriophage.

 

Option C. Transfer of free DNA: Incorrect because this describes transformation, where bacteria take up free or naked DNA from their environment.

 

Option D. Transfer of genome during physical contact: Incorrect because this describes conjugation, where DNA is transferred between bacteria via direct physical contact, typically involving a pilus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lysogenic conversion refers to the acquisition of new properties by a bacterium due to the integration of a bacteriophage's genome into its own DNA, often enhancing bacterial virulence or survival.

questions.stem: Nonenveloped SS-RNA virus is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Picornavirus 

 

Picornavirus is a non-enveloped (naked) RNA virus with a single-stranded RNA genome. It is one of the smallest RNA viruses, which aligns with the mnemonic "PCR" for non-enveloped RNA viruses (Picornavirus, Calicivirus, and Reovirus). The "small baby" analogy helps remember that picornavirus does not "wear clothes" (envelope).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Poxvirus: Incorrect because it is a DNA virus, not an RNA virus. Additionally, it is enveloped.

 

Option C. Retrovirus: Incorrect because although it is an RNA virus, it is enveloped and does not meet the non-enveloped criteria.

 

Option D. Bunyavirus: Incorrect because it is an RNA virus but enveloped, not naked.

 

Note:

 

RNA viruses →15 families →ABCD F2OR3TP2H2

 

  1. Picornavirus: Poliovirus, rhinovirus, hepatitis A virus
  2. Hepevirus: Hepatitis E virus
  3. Calicivirus: Norovirus
  4. Reovirus: Rotavirus
  5. Flavivirus: Yellow fever virus, dengue virus, West Nile virus,HCV
  6. Togavirus: Rubella virus
  7. Retrovirus: HIV, human T-cell leukemia virus
  8. Orthomyxovirus: Influenza virus
  9. Paramyxovirus: Measles virus, mumps virus, RSV
  10. Rhabdovirus: Rabies virus
  11. Filovirus: Ebola virus, Marburg virus
  12. Coronavirus: Coronavirus
  13. Arenavirus: Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus
  14. Bunyavirus: California encephalitis virus, hantavirus
  15. Deltavirus: Hepatitis delta virus

 

DNA viruses → 6 families →HHAPPPy

 

  1. Poxviridae: Variola, vaccinia, cowpox, monkeypox, tanapox, molluscurr contagiosum
  2. Herpesviridae: HSV-1, HSV-2, varicella-zoster, EBV, CMV, HTLV-1, RK-virus
  3. Adenoviride: Adenovirus
  4. Parvoviridae: Parvovirus B19
  5. Papovaviridae: Papilloma virus, Polymavirus
  6. Hepadnaviridae: Hepatitis-B virus

 

 

Educational Objective:


Picornavirus is a small, non-enveloped (naked), single-stranded RNA virus, making it the correct answer. Mnemonics such as "PCR" (Picornavirus, Calicivirus, Reovirus) help to remember the non-enveloped RNA viruses.

questions.stem: The virus with smallest genome is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Parvovirus 

 

Parvovirus has the smallest genome among all viruses. It is a DNA virus with a single-stranded genome. Its genome size is approximately 5 kilobases (kb), making it the smallest genome among both DNA and RNA viruses.

 

Additional Information on Smallest and Largest Genomes:

 

  • Smallest DNA virus: Parvovirus (5 kb, single-stranded DNA).
  • Smallest RNA virus: Picornavirus (7-8 kb, single-stranded RNA).
  • Largest DNA virus: Poxvirus (200-250 kb, double-stranded DNA).
  • Largest RNA virus: Paramyxovirus (150-200 kb, single-stranded RNA).
  • Overall smallest genome: Parvovirus.
  • Overall largest genome: Poxvirus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reovirus: Incorrect because it has a segmented, double-stranded RNA genome with a size of around 23-27 kb.

 

Option C. Picornavirus: Incorrect because although it has the smallest RNA genome (7-8 kb), Parvovirus is smaller.

 

Option D. HIV: Incorrect because its RNA genome (9-10 kb) is larger than both Parvovirus and Picornavirus.

 

Educational Objective:


The smallest viral genome overall is Parvovirus (5 kb, single-stranded DNA). Learn the key distinctions between the smallest and largest genomes in virology for both DNA and RNA viruses.

questions.stem: Von-magnus phenomenon is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) All of above 


The Von-Magnus phenomenon occurs during the replication of certain viruses, notably the influenza virus, and is characterized by defective viral progeny formation. It involves several key aspects:

 

  • Abnormal Replicative Cycle: When multiple influenza viruses infect a single host cell, overcrowding occurs. This leads to a defect in the fifth step of viral replication—the assembly phase. The virus progeny (daughter viruses) are improperly assembled due to this defect.
  • Low Infectivity: The defective progeny have low infectivity because they lack the necessary structural and functional components to effectively infect new host cells.
  • High Hemagglutination: Despite being less infective, the defective progeny often have an increased amount of hemagglutinin (HA) on their surfaces. Hemagglutinin is a glycoprotein that facilitates viral attachment to host cells and contributes to hemagglutination activity.

 

 

Thus, the Von-Magnus phenomenon results in progeny with abnormal replication, low infectivity, and high hemagglutination, making all the options correct.

 

Educational Objective:


The Von-Magnus phenomenon is observed in influenza virus and is characterized by abnormal viral replication, leading to progeny with low infectivity and high hemagglutination activity. All options listed in the question are correct.

questions.stem: Both intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusion is seen in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Measles virus

 

The presence of both intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusion bodies is a distinguishing feature in certain viral infections. Measles virus is notable for this characteristic:

 

  • Measles Virus: The inclusions are known as Warthin-Finkeldey bodies, which are giant multinucleated cells found in lymphoid tissues during measles infection. These bodies are observed both in the cytoplasm and the nucleus, making measles one of the few viruses with this dual inclusion body presence.
  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV): Another virus that exhibits both intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Poxvirus: Incorrect because it produces only cytoplasmic inclusions.

 

Option B. Herpesvirus: Incorrect because it produces only intranuclear inclusions.

 

Option D. Mumps virus: Incorrect because it produces only cytoplasmic inclusions.

 

Educational Objective:


Measles virus is characterized by the presence of both intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Warthin-Finkeldey bodies), making it unique among the options provided.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old male presented with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea of one week duration. The following colonic biopsy is diagnostic of infection with:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Amoebiasis 

 

This is a case of acute abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. The biopsy image provided demonstrates a characteristic flask-shaped ulcer, which is pathognomonic for Amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. This type of ulcer starts in the mucosa and extends into the submucosa, forming a distinctive shape resembling a flower or flask.

 

 

Key Points about Entamoeba histolytica:

 

1. Morphological Forms: It exists in three forms:

 

  • Trophozoite: Amoeboid shape with pseudopodia for motility. It is invasive and responsible for tissue damage.

 

 

  • Pre-cyst: Transitional form.

 

 

  • Cyst: Infective form with a circular shape and four nuclei (mature cyst).

 

 

2. Invasive Mechanism: The trophozoite invades the intestinal wall, forming flask-shaped ulcers. If it spreads via the portal vein, it can cause extraintestinal abscesses, such as the characteristic anchovy sauce abscess in the liver.

 

 

3. Diagnosis:

 

  • Stool Examination: Both cysts and trophozoites can be found in the stool during intestinal amoebiasis.
  • Liver Abscess: Diagnosed via guided aspiration of pus, which contains only trophozoites.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Giardiasis: Incorrect because Giardia lamblia causes non-bloody diarrhea and does not produce flask-shaped ulcers.

 

Option C. Enterobius: Incorrect because Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) primarily causes perianal itching and is not associated with intestinal ulcers.

 

Option D. Severe bacterial infection: Incorrect because bacterial infections like Shigella or Salmonella can cause bloody diarrhea but do not produce flask-shaped ulcers.

 

Educational Objective:


The presence of flask-shaped ulcers in a colonic biopsy is diagnostic of Amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. The infective form is the quadrinucleated cyst, and the invasive form is the trophozoite.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl residing in a village recently returned from a vacation visiting her friends in another village. She complained of severe headache and fever, was diagnosed as a case of pyogenic meningitis and admitted to the hospital. She died 5 days later. Which of the following organism should be considered in the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Naegleria fowleri 


This case highlights a fatal condition misdiagnosed as pyogenic meningitis. The correct diagnosis is primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) caused by Naegleria fowleri.

 

Key Clues:

 

  • The patient is a 15-year-old girl who recently returned from a vacation.
  • She presented with headache, fever, and symptoms of meningitis.
  • Despite being treated for pyogenic meningitis, she deteriorated and died within 5 days.
  • Naegleria fowleri is associated with exposure to contaminated freshwater (e.g., swimming during a vacation), which aligns with the case history.

 

Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM):

 

  • PAM is caused by Naegleria fowleri, a free-living amoeba found in warm freshwater.
  • The amoeba enters through the nasal passages during swimming or water activities and migrates to the brain via the olfactory nerve.
  • Symptoms mimic bacterial meningitis but progress rapidly, leading to severe brain inflammation and death in most cases within 5-7 days.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Entamoeba histolytica: Incorrect because it causes intestinal and hepatic infections, not meningitis.

 

Option C. Toxoplasma gondii: Incorrect because it causes toxoplasmosis, which is typically subacute or chronic, not rapidly fatal.

 

Option D. Falciparum malaria: Incorrect because cerebral malaria can cause neurological symptoms, but it does not present as meningitis and would typically improve with appropriate antimalarial treatment.

 

Educational Objective:


Naegleria fowleri is a neuroparasite causing primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), which is rapidly fatal and often associated with swimming in contaminated freshwater. It should be suspected in cases of acute meningitis with a history of freshwater exposure.

questions.stem: Host harboring adult or sexual stage of a parasite is called:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Definitive host 

 

The host in which the adult or sexual stage of a parasite resides is referred to as the definitive host. This distinction is important in understanding the life cycle of parasites, as different stages of the parasite’s development occur in specific hosts.

 

Key Definitions:

 

Definitive Host:

 

  • For protozoan parasites (unicellular): The host harboring the sexual form of the parasite.
  • For helminths (metazoan, multicellular): The host harboring the adult form of the parasite.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Intermediate Host:

 

  • For protozoan parasites: The host harboring the asexual form of the parasite.
  • For helminths: The host harboring the larval form of the parasite.

 

Option C. Reservoir Host: A host that harbors the parasite and serves as a source of infection for others but is not necessary for the parasite’s life cycle.

 

Educational Objective:


A definitive host is the host in which the adult or sexual stage of a parasite is found. This definition applies to both protozoan and metazoan parasites. For the intermediate host, it’s the asexual or larval stages that are present.

questions.stem: The cystic form of all are seen in man except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Trichomonas 

 

Most protozoa exhibit both trophozoite and cystic forms in their life cycle. The trophozoite is the active, feeding stage, while the cyst is a dormant, resistant stage that facilitates survival outside the host and transmission to new hosts. However, Trichomonas vaginalis, a protozoan parasite, does not have a cystic form. Instead, it exists only in the trophozoite form, which is responsible for infection and transmission.

 

 

 

Trichomonas vaginalis and other similar parasites rely on direct transmission methods (e.g., sexual contact) and thus do not require a cystic form for survival outside the host.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. E. histolytica: Entamoeba histolytica has both trophozoite and cyst forms. The cyst form is the infectious stage and can survive harsh environmental conditions, allowing fecal-oral transmission.

 

Option B. Giardia: Giardia lamblia also has both trophozoite and cyst forms. The cyst stage is crucial for its transmission through contaminated food or water.

 

Option D. Toxoplasma: Toxoplasma gondii produces cysts during its life cycle, particularly in tissue, as part of its persistence in the host. These cysts are important for its transmission, especially through undercooked meat or contaminated soil.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The only protozoan parasite in the given options that lacks a cystic form and exists solely as a trophozoite is Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.stem: Vector for T. cruzi is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Reduviid bug

 

The vector for Trypanosoma cruzi is the Reduviid bug, also known as the "kissing bug." The transmission occurs when the bug defecates on the skin of the host during or after taking a blood meal. The infective form of the parasite, the trypomastigote, is present in the feces of the Reduviid bug. When the host rubs or scratches the bite site, the feces containing the trypomastigote are introduced into the wound, allowing the parasite to enter the host’s bloodstream.

 

 

Importantly, the saliva of the Reduviid bug does not contain the parasite. The bug's unusual feeding habit—defecating before or during a blood meal—plays a critical role in the transmission of T. cruzi. This behavior facilitates contamination of the wound with infected feces, leading to infection.

 

Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease, characterized by acute symptoms such as fever and swelling at the site of entry, and chronic complications, including cardiac and gastrointestinal disorders.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Tsetse fly: Incorrect. The Tsetse fly is the vector for Trypanosoma brucei, which causes African sleeping sickness, not T. cruzi.

 

 

Option C. Sand fly: Incorrect. The Sand fly transmits Leishmania species, causing leishmaniasis, not T. cruzi.

 

 

Option D. Hard tick: Incorrect. Hard ticks are vectors for diseases like Lyme disease and babesiosis, but they are not associated with T. cruzi.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The vector for Trypanosoma cruzi is the Reduviid bug, and transmission occurs through contact with feces containing the infective trypomastigote, not via saliva. This unique transmission mechanism is a key feature of Chagas disease.

questions.stem: How many pairs of flagella does Giardia lamblia possess?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Four 

 

Giardia lamblia is a flagellate protozoan and the only intestinal flagellate found in humans. The trophozoite form of G. lamblia possesses four pairs of flagella, making a total of eight flagella. These flagella are crucial for its motility, which is characterized by a "falling leaf" motion.

 

  • The trophozoite is tear-drop shaped, also described as resembling a badminton or tennis racket.
  • The organism exhibits bilateral symmetry: each component, including its nuclei, sucking discs, and axonemes, is mirrored on both sides.

 

The cyst form of G. lamblia is quadrinucleate, meaning it contains four nuclei. This form is the infective stage, transmitted via ingestion of contaminated food or water.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. One: Incorrect. G. lamblia has four pairs of flagella, not one pair.

 

Option B. Two: Incorrect. Two pairs of flagella are insufficient to describe the anatomy of G. lamblia, which clearly possesses four pairs.

 

Option C. Three: Incorrect. The organism is described as having four pairs of flagella, making a total of eight flagella. Three pairs would not be consistent with its anatomy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Giardia lamblia possesses four pairs of flagella (eight in total), and its characteristic motility is described as "falling leaf" motion. This key fact is essential for identifying the organism.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with acute watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps. Stool microscopy reveals trophozoites with falling leaf motility. The etiological agent is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Giardia lamblia 

 

The presence of trophozoites with falling leaf motility is characteristic of Giardia lamblia. This organism is a flagellate protozoan that infects the small intestine and is a common cause of diarrhea in children.

 

 

  • The infection begins when a child ingests food or water contaminated with the infective stage, the quadrinucleate cyst.
  • Once ingested, excystation occurs in the duodenum and jejunum, releasing trophozoites. Unlike Entamoeba histolytica, which invades tissues, Giardia lamblia trophozoites remain in the intestinal lumen and adhere to the villi.
  • The trophozoites disrupt the normal function of the villi, leading to malabsorption of nutrients. This manifests as watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and malabsorption syndrome.
  • The infection is particularly common in young children due to poor hygiene and increased exposure to contaminated sources.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Entamoeba histolytica: Incorrect. E. histolytica causes invasive amoebiasis with symptoms such as dysentery and abscess formation. It does not display falling leaf motility.

 

Option C. Trichomonas tenax: Incorrect. T. tenax is a flagellate found in the oral cavity and does not cause intestinal infections or diarrhea.

 

Option D. Balantidium coli: Incorrect. B. coli causes balantidiasis, which is characterized by large intestinal ulceration. Its motility is ciliary, not falling leaf.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of trophozoites with falling leaf motility in stool microscopy strongly indicates Giardia lamblia as the etiological agent, which causes watery diarrhea and malabsorption syndrome.

questions.stem: Ziemann’s stippling of erythrocyte is caused by which species of plasmodium?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Malariae 

 

Ziemann’s stippling refers to the specific stippling or dot-like appearance in erythrocytes caused by the presence of Plasmodium malariae. When the parasite infects red blood cells (RBCs), it metabolizes hemoglobin and causes the appearance of fine pigment granules known as Ziemann's dots.

 

Key points to remember:

 

  • These stipplings are distinctive for Plasmodium malariae.
  • The dots are formed as part of the parasite’s metabolic processes within the RBC.
  • This phenomenon can be observed under a microscope, aiding in the identification of the species causing malaria.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Vivax: Incorrect. P. vivax is associated with Schöffner’s dots, not Ziemann’s stippling.

 

Option B. Falciparum: Incorrect. P. falciparum exhibits Maurer’s dots, not Ziemann’s stippling.

 

Option D. Ovale: Incorrect. P. ovale shows James’ dots, not Ziemann’s stippling.

 

Mnemonic to Remember:

 

Use the mnemonic "Very Fantastic Medical Officer" to correlate the Plasmodium species with their respective stippling:

 

  • Very: Vivax – Schöffner’s dots
  • Fantastic: Falciparum – Maurer’s dots
  • Medical: Malariae – Ziemann’s dots
  • Officer: Ovale – James’ dots

 

You can also think of "See More Zebra in Jungle" to remember:

 

  • See: Schöffner’s dots (Vivax)
  • More: Maurer’s dots (Falciparum)
  • Zebra: Ziemann’s dots (Malariae)
  • Jungle: James’ dots (Ovale)

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ziemann’s stippling is a hallmark feature of Plasmodium malariae. Learn the differences in stippling patterns to accurately identify the species causing malaria.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with complaints of dysphagia. On UGI Endoscopy a diagnosis of esophageal candidiasis was made. The organism obtained from the sample was cultured on a specialized media and the below finding were visible on microscopy of the culture. What phenomenon is shown below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Germ tube formation 

 

The image shows the characteristic germ tube formation, which is a diagnostic feature of Candida albicans. The germ tube test, also known as the Reynolds-Brute phenomenon, is used to differentiate Candida albicans from other Candida species.

 

Key points about the germ tube test:

 

  • When Candida albicans is incubated in serum or plasma at 37°C for 2-3 hours, it forms germ tubes, which are filamentous projections without constrictions at the junction.
  • This test is highly specific for Candida albicans, as other Candida species are germ tube-negative.

 

Clinical relevance:

 

  • Esophageal candidiasis is a common infection in immunocompromised patients and is often caused by Candida albicans. The germ tube test is an important tool in confirming the species.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Spore formation: Incorrect because spores are reproductive structures formed by fungi, not related to germ tube formation.

 

Option C. Mould to yeast formation: Incorrect because this refers to dimorphic fungi (e.g., Histoplasma capsulatum) and is not observed in Candida albicans.

 

Option D. Budding: Incorrect because budding refers to the formation of daughter cells in yeast, which is a general feature of most yeasts, including Candida species, but not specific to germ tube formation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The germ tube test is specific for Candida albicans and helps differentiate it from other Candida species, showing filamentous germ tube structures after incubation in serum.

questions.stemHtml: The image given below belongs which of the following organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cryptococcus 

 

The image shows characteristic features of Cryptococcus, a capsulated fungus. The following clues are essential for its identification:

 

  1. Capsulated fungus: Cryptococcus is the only medically important fungus with a thick polysaccharide capsule, visible in the image.
  2. India ink preparation: The background appears black due to the negative staining technique (India ink), which highlights the capsule as a clear halo surrounding the yeast cells.

 

Clinical relevance:

 

  • Cryptococcus, particularly Cryptococcus neoformans, is an opportunistic pathogen commonly associated with meningitis in immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV/AIDS.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Candida: Incorrect because Candida species do not possess a capsule and appear as budding yeast or pseudohyphae.

 

Option C. Histoplasma: Incorrect because Histoplasma capsulatum appears as small, intracellular yeast in infected macrophages and does not have a capsule.

 

Option D. Blastomyces: Incorrect because Blastomyces dermatitidis is a dimorphic fungus that forms thick-walled yeast but lacks a capsule.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cryptococcus is a capsulated fungus identified by its thick capsule visible in India ink preparation, which appears as a clear halo around the yeast cells.

questions.stem: Which of the organisms is responsible for orbital cellulitis in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Mucor 

 

Orbital cellulitis in a diabetic patient, especially one with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), is most commonly caused by Mucor species, leading to mucormycosis.

 

 

  • Mucormycosis is an aggressive fungal infection caused by members of the Mucorales order, such as Rhizopus and Mucor species.
  • It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, including patients with diabetes, organ transplant recipients, and those on prolonged corticosteroid therapy.
  • Involvement of the orbit is a hallmark of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis.

 

Pathophysiology:

 

  • The fungus has a strong affinity for blood vessels, causing tissue necrosis and rapid invasion into surrounding structures.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cryptococcus: Incorrect because Cryptococcus primarily causes meningitis and does not commonly involve the orbit.

 

Option B. Candida: Incorrect because Candida usually causes mucocutaneous infections or systemic candidiasis, not orbital cellulitis.

 

Option D. Aspergillus: Incorrect because although Aspergillus can cause orbital infections, it is more common in prolonged neutropenia and does not have as strong an association with DKA as Mucor species.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mucormycosis is the most common fungal cause of orbital cellulitis in diabetic or immunosuppressed patients, especially in the presence of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.stem: Biochemical analysis of pyogenic meningitis reveals all of the following, except:

options.label: B
options.text: Total leukocyte count: Highly elevated, neutrophilic

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Glucose: highly elevated 

 

In pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis, the biochemical analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) typically shows the following:

 

  • CSF pressure: Highly elevated due to inflammation and increased intracranial pressure.
  • Total leukocyte count: Elevated with a predominance of neutrophils, reflecting the bacterial infection.
  • Total proteins: Markedly increased because bacterial cell walls are made of proteins, and the inflammatory response also releases proteins into the CSF.
  • Glucose: Reduced (not elevated). This is because bacteria in the CSF consume glucose as a source of energy, leading to decreased glucose levels.

 

Key reasoning:

 

  • In meningitis, glucose levels are consistently decreased due to bacterial metabolism. It is never elevated in any form of meningitis, including bacterial, viral, or fungal.
  • Protein levels rise due to the breakdown of the blood-CSF barrier and the presence of bacterial proteins.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In pyogenic meningitis, glucose levels in the CSF are decreased, not elevated, due to bacterial consumption of glucose as a nutrient.

questions.stem: MCC of catheter induced UTI:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) E. coli

 

The most common cause (MCC) of catheter-induced urinary tract infections (UTIs), as well as UTIs in general, is E. coli. This is true irrespective of the patient’s age, gender, or underlying condition.

 

Why E. coli is the MCC:

 

  • E. coli has specialized virulence factors, including adhesins (type 1 pili and P fimbriae) that facilitate attachment to the urothelial lining and catheter surfaces.
  • It forms biofilms on catheters, which makes it particularly resistant to clearance and antibiotics.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Klebsiella: Incorrect because it is less commonly isolated than E. coli in catheter-induced UTIs.

 

Option C. Pseudomonas: Incorrect because it is associated with hospital-acquired infections but is not the most common cause.

 

Option D. Staphylococcus: Incorrect because Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a less frequent cause of UTIs and more often associated with young, sexually active females rather than catheter-induced cases.

 

Educational Objective:

 

E. coli is the most common cause of UTIs, including catheter-induced UTIs, due to its ability to adhere to the urinary tract and form biofilms.

questions.stemHtml: A Female had a thorn prick 5 years ago. She presented with a slowly growing 2 × 2 cm verrucous lesion which on KOH mount showed the following image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Chromoblastomycosis

 

The patient’s presentation and the KOH mount findings provide critical clues:

 

  1. Thorn prick history: A common route of entry for subcutaneous mycoses.
  2. Verrucous lesion: A hallmark clinical feature of chromoblastomycosis.
  3. KOH mount image: Shows characteristic brown, circular structures with septa resembling "copper pennies" or "Medlar bodies," which are diagnostic for chromoblastomycosis.

 

Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (dark-pigmented) fungi, which enter the body through traumatic implantation, such as a thorn prick. Over time, the lesion grows slowly and presents with the described features.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phaeohyphomycosis: Incorrect because this condition involves pigmented hyphae but does not form copper pennies or Medlar bodies.

 

Option B. Blastomycosis: Incorrect because it primarily causes systemic disease and lacks the copper penny structures.

 

Option C. Sporotrichosis: Incorrect because it typically presents with linear nodular lesions along lymphatic channels, not verrucous lesions with Medlar bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Chromoblastomycosis is characterized by verrucous lesions and the presence of copper pennies (Medlar bodies) on KOH mount, often following traumatic implantation such as a thorn prick.

questions.stem: Rhinosporidium seeberi belongs to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Aquatic protistan protozoa 

 

Initially, Rhinosporidium seeberi was thought to be a fungus. However, genetic analysis has revealed that it is not a fungus but rather an aquatic protistan parasite. This discovery has reclassified it under aquatic protistan protozoa. Although some older references may still list it as a fungus, this categorization is outdated.

 

Clinical presentation:

 

  • Rhinosporidium seeberi primarily causes fragile, bleeding nasal polyps.
  • It can also involve other mucosal sites, but nasal polyps are the hallmark presentation.

 

Laboratory diagnosis:

 

  • The presence of large spherules containing endospores is a diagnostic feature.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fungus: Incorrect because Rhinosporidium seeberi has been reclassified as a protistan protozoa.

 

Option B. Bacteria: Incorrect because it is not a bacterial organism.

 

Option D. Virus: Incorrect because Rhinosporidium seeberi is not a viral pathogen.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Rhinosporidium seeberi is an aquatic protistan protozoa that causes nasal polyps and is characterized by spherules with endospores on microscopic examination.

questions.stem: Cigar body is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Sporotrichosis 

 

Cigar bodies, also known as asteroid bodies, are a diagnostic feature of sporotrichosis, a subcutaneous fungal infection caused by Sporothrix schenckii. These structures appear as elongated, cigar-shaped yeast cells under the microscope.

 

Clinical presentation:

 

  • Sporotrichosis is often referred to as "rose gardener's disease" because it typically occurs following a thorn prick or similar injury while handling vegetation.

 

 

  • The infection spreads along lymphatic channels, causing a characteristic linear or serial pattern of nodular lesions.

 

Other features:

 

 

  • Cigar bodies are seen in tissue specimens from affected individuals.
  • The disease involves subcutaneous tissues and lymphatics, but does not present with verrucous lesions like chromoblastomycosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cryptococcosis: Incorrect because it is caused by Cryptococcus neoformans and does not produce cigar-shaped bodies.

 

Option C. Histoplasmosis: Incorrect because it is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, which forms intracellular oval yeast, not cigar bodies.

 

Option D. Aspergillosis: Incorrect because it is caused by Aspergillus species and presents with hyphae, not yeast cells or cigar bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cigar bodies (asteroid bodies) are a hallmark feature of sporotrichosis, a fungal infection commonly seen in individuals exposed to thorn pricks or handling vegetation.

questions.stem: Darling disease is caused by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Histoplasma 

 

Darling disease is another name for histoplasmosis, a fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. The disease is named after the scientist Samuel Darling, who first described it.

 

Clinical features:

 

  • The infection primarily affects the lungs, presenting with symptoms similar to tuberculosis, such as cough, fever, and weight loss.
  • Disseminated histoplasmosis may occur in immunocompromised individuals, affecting other organs such as the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

 

Pathogenesis:

 

  • Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that exists as a mould in the environment and as yeast in human tissues.
  • Infection typically occurs through inhalation of spores found in soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Candida: Incorrect because Candida species cause candidiasis, which primarily presents as mucocutaneous infections or systemic infections in immunocompromised patients.

 

Option C. Cryptococcus: Incorrect because Cryptococcus neoformans causes cryptococcosis, often presenting as meningitis in immunocompromised individuals.

 

Option D. Rhizopus: Incorrect because Rhizopus species cause mucormycosis, a rapidly progressive fungal infection affecting sinuses and brain, particularly in diabetics or immunosuppressed individuals.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Darling disease is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum and primarily affects the lungs, with potential for dissemination in immunocompromised patients.

questions.stemHtml: Histopathological image given below belongs to which of the following fungus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Blastomyces 

 

The histopathological image provided shows the characteristic "figure of eight" appearance, which is a hallmark of blastomycosis. This fungal infection is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis, also known as North American blastomycosis, Gilchrist’s disease, or Chicago disease.

 

Key features of the image:

 

  • Figure of eight appearance: The fungal elements show a double-contoured, thick-walled structure.
  • Thick double wall: This feature distinguishes it from other fungi.

 

Clinical features:

 

  • Blastomycosis primarily affects the lungs and can disseminate to the skin, bones, and other organs.
  • It is commonly associated with areas near rivers or lakes in North America.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Histoplasma: Incorrect because Histoplasma capsulatum typically appears as small, intracellular yeast within macrophages and does not have the thick double wall or figure of eight appearance.

 

Option C. Coccidioides: Incorrect because Coccidioides species form spherules containing endospores, not thick-walled yeasts with a figure of eight appearance.

 

Option D. Paracoccidioides: Incorrect because Paracoccidioides brasiliensis produces a characteristic "pilot’s wheel" appearance, distinct from the figure of eight seen in blastomycosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The "figure of eight" appearance with a thick double wall in histopathological images is diagnostic of blastomycosis caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis.

questions.stem: Thirty-eight children consumed eatables procured from a single source at a picnic party. Twenty children developed abdominal cramps followed by vomiting and watery diarrhea 6–10 hours after the party. The most likely etiology for the outbreak is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Clostridium perfringens infection 

 

  • The incubation period in the question falls in the 8–16 hour range, making Clostridium perfringens the most likely causative agent.
  • Symptoms match with Clostridium perfringens food poisoning, which is associated with poorly cooked or stored food  and the symptoms of abdominal cramps, vomiting, and watery diarrhea.

 

Classification of food poisoning based on incubation period:

 

  1. 1–6 hours:
    • Caused by preformed toxins.
    • Common organisms: Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus (emetic type).
  2. 8–16 hours:
    • Caused by organisms producing toxins after ingestion.
    • Common organisms: Clostridium perfringens and Bacillus cereus (diarrheal type).
  3. >16 hours:
    • Caused by organisms like Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC), Vibrio species, and others.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rotavirus infection: Incorrect because rotavirus has a longer incubation period and primarily affects infants and young children, presenting with fever and dehydration.

 

Option B. Enterotoxigenic E. coli infection: Incorrect because it typically has an incubation period >16 hours and is associated with travel-related diarrhea.

 

Option C. Staphylococcal toxin: Incorrect because it causes symptoms within 1–6 hours due to preformed toxins.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Food poisoning caused by Clostridium perfringens typically presents with symptoms after an incubation period of 8–16 hours, including abdominal cramps, vomiting, and watery diarrhea.

questions.stem: EBV action in nasopharynx is through:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) CD 21

 

Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) is also known as the kissing virus due to its transmission through saliva. EBV primarily targets B lymphocytes and epithelial cells in the nasopharynx and tonsils by binding to CD21, also known as the C3d receptor. This receptor is expressed on the surface of B cells and epithelial cells, facilitating viral entry.

 

Key features of EBV:

 

  • Primary target cells: EBV infects B lymphocytes and nasopharyngeal epithelial cells.
  • Entry mechanism: The virus binds to CD21 on B cells, enabling viral internalization.
  • LMP protein production: After entering the B cell, EBV produces latent membrane protein (LMP), which makes the infected cell immortal.
  • Disease association:
    • Benign disease: Infectious mononucleosis (characterized by fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy).
    • Malignant disease: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and certain Hodgkin's and non-Hodgkin's lymphomas.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. CD3: Incorrect because CD3 is associated with T cells, not B cells. EBV does not target CD3.

 

Option B. CD4: Incorrect because CD4 is a receptor on helper T cells, targeted by HIV, not EBV.

 

Option C. CD8: Incorrect because CD8 is a receptor on cytotoxic T cells, which play a role in immune response but are not directly targeted by EBV.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) enters B lymphocytes and epithelial cells through the CD21 receptor, leading to both benign (infectious mononucleosis) and malignant conditions (e.g., Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma).

questions.stem: Paul Bunnell test for:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Infectious mononucleosis

 

The Paul Bunnell test is a type of heterophile agglutination test used to diagnose infectious mononucleosis, a condition caused by the Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV). It detects heterophile antibodies in the patient's serum, which are produced in response to EBV infection and cross-react with antigens on sheep red blood cells (RBCs).

 

Key features of the test:

 

  • Principle: The patient's serum containing heterophile antibodies (if present) agglutinates sheep RBCs due to molecular mimicry between antigens on EBV and sheep RBCs.

 

 

  • Specificity: These heterophile antibodies are not directly formed against sheep RBCs but react due to the similarity of antigens, demonstrating cross-reactivity (molecular mimicry).
  • Usefulness: A positive agglutination test confirms the presence of EBV-induced heterophile antibodies, supporting a diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Malta fever (Brucellosis): Incorrect because Malta fever is caused by Brucella species, and the diagnosis is made via serology, such as the Rose Bengal test, or by culture. Paul Bunnell test is not used.

 

Option B. Typhus fever: Incorrect because typhus fever is caused by Rickettsia species, and the diagnosis involves serologic tests like the Weil-Felix test, not Paul Bunnell test.

 

Option C. Enteric fever (Typhoid): Incorrect because enteric fever is caused by Salmonella typhi, and diagnosis involves blood or stool cultures or serologic tests like the Widal test.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Paul Bunnell test detects heterophile antibodies in the serum and is a diagnostic test for infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).

questions.stem: Segmented genome is found in all, except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Rhabdovirus 

 

A segmented genome means the viral RNA is divided into multiple fragments. Among the 15 RNA virus families, only four have segmented genomes. The mnemonic "BORA" helps to remember them:

 

  • B for Bunyavirus: Segmented into 3 pieces.
  • O for Orthomyxovirus (e.g., Influenza virus): Segmented into 8 pieces.
  • R for Reovirus: Segmented into 10-12 pieces.
  • A for Arenavirus: Segmented into 2 pieces.

 

Rhabdovirus, on the other hand, has a non-segmented RNA genome, which makes it the correct answer to this question.

 

Additional Information on Segmented Viruses:

 

  • Segmented genomes allow for genetic reassortment, which can result in rapid genetic variation and new strains of viruses, especially evident in Influenza virus.
  • Bunyavirus: Known for causing diseases such as Hantavirus and Rift Valley fever.
  • Orthomyxovirus: Influenza virus, responsible for seasonal flu and pandemics.
  • Reovirus: Includes Rotavirus, a leading cause of diarrhea in children.
  • Arenavirus: Includes Lassa fever virus.

 

Educational Objective:


Among RNA viruses, the four with segmented genomes are remembered by the mnemonic "BORA" (Bunyavirus, Orthomyxovirus, Reovirus, Arenavirus). Rhabdovirus is non-segmented and does not belong to this group.

questions.stem: Slapped cheek appearance with fever is seen in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Parvovirus B19 

 

Parvovirus B19 is the causative agent of erythema infectiosum, also known as the fifth disease. It presents with a characteristic slapped cheek appearance, where the child’s cheeks appear red as if they were slapped, accompanied by fever. This is a hallmark clinical feature in children.

 

Key features of Parvovirus B19:

 

  1. Smallest virus: It is the smallest known DNA virus.
  2. Unique DNA structure: It is the only single-stranded DNA virus, making it an exception among DNA viruses.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rubella: Incorrect because rubella (German measles) causes a maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads downward but does not result in a slapped cheek appearance.

 

Option B. Rubeola: Incorrect because rubeola (measles) presents with Koplik’s spots in the oral cavity and a maculopapular rash, not with the slapped cheek appearance.

 

Option D. HSV-6: Incorrect because human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) causes roseola infantum (exanthem subitum), which presents with a sudden onset of high fever followed by a macular rash on the body, not a slapped cheek rash.

 

Additional Information

 

Parvovirus B19 Clinical Presentations:

 

 

  1. Children:
    • Slapped cheek appearance: Erythema on cheeks with a lacy rash on the extremities.
    • Known as fifth disease or erythema infectiosum.
  2. Adults:
    • Arthritis/Arthropathy: Pain and swelling in small joints, particularly in the wrists, knees, and ankles.
  3. Fetuses:
    • Causes hydrops fetalis due to severe anemia, leading to fetal heart failure and possibly miscarriage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Slapped cheek appearance in children is pathognomonic of erythema infectiosum, caused by Parvovirus B19, the smallest DNA virus and the only single-stranded DNA virus.

questions.stem: Eggs of which of the following parasite cause intense pruritus in perianal skin:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Enterobius vermicularis 

 

The eggs of Enterobius vermicularis (commonly known as the pinworm) are the cause of intense pruritus (itching) in the perianal region, particularly at night. This is a hallmark feature of pinworm infection and is caused by the following life cycle:

 

 

  1. Adult Worms in the Intestine: The adult worms reside in the rectum and colon of the infected individual.
  2. Nighttime Egg-Laying: At night, the gravid female worm migrates to the perianal region to lay eggs. The eggs are sticky and irritate the skin, causing intense pruritus.
  3. Auto-Infection: When the child scratches the perianal area, eggs contaminate the fingers and fingernails. These eggs are then ingested when the child puts their fingers in their mouth, perpetuating the cycle.
  4. Infective Form: The eggs are the infective form and hatch in the intestine, releasing larvae that mature into adult worms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ascaris: Incorrect. Ascaris lumbricoides eggs are ingested through contaminated food or water and do not cause perianal pruritus.

 

Option B. Hookworm: Incorrect. Hookworm infection causes anemia and gastrointestinal symptoms, but it does not lead to perianal itching. The infective larvae penetrate the skin.

 

Option D. Trichuris: Incorrect. Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) causes diarrhea and rectal prolapse in severe cases but does not result in perianal pruritus.

 

Key Clinical Feature:

 

  • Nocturnal perianal pruritus is diagnostic of Enterobius vermicularis infection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The eggs of Enterobius vermicularis cause intense perianal pruritus, especially at night, due to the female worm's egg-laying behavior. This leads to auto-infection and a continuous cycle in the host.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is implicated in the causation of botryomycosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Staphylococcus aureus 

 

Botryomycosis is a chronic bacterial infection that mimics fungal infections but is caused by bacteria, primarily Staphylococcus aureus. This condition typically involves the skin and subcutaneous tissues and is characterized by the formation of sinuses and discharging granules, which are colonies of bacteria. Despite its name, botryomycosis is not caused by fungi but by bacteria.

 

Types of Mycetomas:

 

  1. Eumycetoma: Caused by fungi.
  2. Actinomycetoma: Caused by bacteria from the Actinomyces species.
  3. Botryomycosis: Caused by bacteria, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus.

 

 

In botryomycosis, the classic triad includes:

 

  • Tumefaction (tumor-like swelling).
  • Multiple discharging sinuses.
  • Presence of granules (colored colonies of bacteria).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Staphylococcus albus: Incorrect because this bacterium is not typically implicated in botryomycosis.

 

Option C. Streptococcus pneumonia: Incorrect because it primarily causes respiratory infections, not botryomycosis.

 

Option D. Streptococcus pyogenes: Incorrect because it is primarily associated with pharyngitis and skin infections but not botryomycosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Botryomycosis is a bacterial infection caused primarily by Staphylococcus aureus and is often misinterpreted as a fungal infection due to its name and clinical presentation.

questions.stem: Consumption of uncooked beef is likely to cause which of the following helminthic diseases:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Taenia saginata 

 

The consumption of uncooked beef is associated with Taenia saginata infection, commonly referred to as beef tapeworm. Here are the key details:

 

  • Source: Taenia saginata infection occurs when the larval form, Cysticercus bovis, present in the muscle of cattle (beef), is ingested by humans in undercooked or raw meat.
  • Unarmed Tapeworm: T. saginata is termed "unarmed" because its scolex (head) has four suckers but lacks a rostellum and hooks.
  • Lifecycle: After ingestion, the larvae mature into adult tapeworms in the human intestine, where they attach to the intestinal wall using their suckers. They grow, producing proglottids (segments) that are released in feces.
  • Symptoms: Most cases are asymptomatic, but infected individuals may experience abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, or malnutrition.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Taenia solium: Incorrect. T. solium (pork tapeworm) is transmitted through the consumption of undercooked pork, not beef. Its larval form, Cysticercus cellulosae, is found in the muscle of pigs. Additionally, T. solium is "armed," as its scolex has a rostellum with hooks.

 

Option C. Hydatid cyst: Incorrect. Hydatid disease is caused by Echinococcus granulosus or E. multilocularis, not by Taenia species. The primary hosts are canines, and transmission occurs through ingestion of eggs in contaminated food or water, not by consuming beef.

 

Option D. Trichuris trichiura: Incorrect. T. trichiura (whipworm) is not transmitted through the consumption of meat. It is acquired by ingesting embryonated eggs in contaminated soil or food.

 

Key Differences Between Taenia saginata and Taenia solium:

 

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Consumption of uncooked beef causes Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) infection. The infective form is the Cysticercus bovis, found in the muscles of cattle.

questions.stemHtml: Following type of eggs are seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Schistosoma mansoni 

 

The egg depicted in the image shows a lateral spine, which is a defining feature of Schistosoma mansoni. Learning the distinct features of eggs from various Schistosoma species is critical for accurate identification.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Schistosoma haematobium: The egg has a terminal spine and is typically found in urine samples. This species is associated with urinary schistosomiasis and can cause urinary bladder carcinoma (oncogenic).

 

 

Option C. Schistosoma japonicum: The egg features a small knob rather than a spine. It is also found in stool samples and causes intestinal schistosomiasis, often more severe due to higher egg production.

 

 

Option D. Clonorchis sinensis: This species does not produce eggs with spines or knobs. Its eggs are operculated and are associated with liver fluke infections.

 

 

Key Clinical Features:

 

  • Schistosoma haematobium: Causes hematuria, dysuria, and is linked to urinary bladder carcinoma.
  • Schistosoma mansoni: Causes intestinal schistosomiasis, manifesting as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly.
  • Schistosoma japonicum: Causes more severe intestinal disease due to higher egg output, often leading to hepatosplenomegaly and fibrosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The presence of a lateral spine on the egg is diagnostic of Schistosoma mansoni.
  • Differentiate Schistosoma species by their egg morphology:
    • Terminal spine: Schistosoma haematobium
    • Lateral spine: Schistosoma mansoni
    • Knob: Schistosoma japonicum.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the organism from its egg in the picture?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Necator americanus 

 

The egg shown in the image is characterized by:

 

Four Blastomeres: The egg contains four distinct blastomeres, which is a classic feature of hookworm eggs.

 

Non-Bile-Stained Appearance: The egg is not yellow in color, indicating that it is bile-negative. This is a key diagnostic clue since only a few helminth eggs are bile-negative.

 

Mnemonic to Remember Bile-Negative Eggs: Use the mnemonic "NEHA":

 

  • N: Necator americanus (hookworm)
  • E: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm)
  • H: Hymenolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm)
  • A: Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm)

 

From the mnemonic, and based on the egg morphology in the image, the correct answer is Necator americanus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Enterobius vermicularis: Incorrect. E. vermicularis eggs are elongated and flattened on one side, resembling a "D" shape. They are not associated with four blastomeres.

 

Option B. Trichuris trichiura: Incorrect. T. trichiura eggs are barrel-shaped and possess polar plugs at both ends, which are absent in the given image.

 

Option C. Ascaris lumbricoides: Incorrect. A. lumbricoides eggs are bile-stained and have a thick, rough outer shell. The given egg is not bile-stained and lacks the characteristic shell.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The egg with four blastomeres and a non-bile-stained appearance is diagnostic of Necator americanus, a hookworm species that causes iron-deficiency anemia through chronic blood loss in infected individuals.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old female presented to the OPD with pain in the anogenital region. On examination, multiple warts were seen. A suspicion of HPV infection, a genetic analysis was done which showed that she is at high risk of invasive CA cervix. Which of the following type of HPV is responsible for this?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) HPV 18

 

Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is a DNA virus belonging to the Papillomaviridae family, which is responsible for both benign and malignant lesions. Among the HPV types, specific serotypes are associated with a high risk of malignancy, particularly cervical cancer.

 

Key points about high-risk HPV:

 

  • High-risk types: HPV 16, 18, 31, 33, 45 are strongly associated with invasive cervical cancer. Among these, HPV 16 and 18 are the most common culprits, with HPV18 being included in this question.
  • Low-risk types: HPV 6 and 11 are associated with benign anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata) and laryngeal papillomatosis but do not cause cancer.
  • Mechanism of oncogenesis:
    • HPV produces E6 and E7 oncoproteins.
    • E6: Leads to the degradation of p53, a tumor suppressor gene.
    • E7: Inactivates the retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor gene.
    • This results in uncontrolled cell division, leading to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and invasive cervical cancer.

 

 

In this case, the patient presents with multiple warts and is at high risk of cervical cancer, strongly pointing to HPV18 as the causative agent.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. HPV1: Incorrect because HPV1 is associated with benign lesions like verruca plantaris (plantar warts), which occur on the sole of the feet, and not anogenital lesions.

 

Option B. HPV5: Incorrect because HPV5 is associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis, a rare condition characterized by skin lesions, but not with anogenital warts or cervical cancer.

 

Option C. HPV11: Incorrect because HPV11 is a low-risk HPV type that causes benign anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata) and laryngeal papillomatosis, not cervical cancer.

 

 

Additional Information

 

  • HPV and cancer: HPV is responsible for almost all cases of cervical cancer, along with a subset of anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers.
  • Prevention: HPV vaccines (e.g., Gardasil) target high-risk serotypes such as HPV16 and HPV18, as well as low-risk types HPV6 and HPV11, reducing the incidence of cervical cancer and genital warts.

 

Educational Objective:

 

HPV16 and HPV18 are high-risk types associated with cervical cancer, while HPV6 and HPV11 are low-risk types that cause benign warts. In this case, the high-risk HPV type responsible is HPV18.

questions.stem: Winter bottom sign in sleeping sickness refers to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy 

 

Winterbottom sign is a clinical feature associated with African trypanosomiasis, also known as sleeping sickness, caused by Trypanosoma brucei. It refers to the posterior cervical lymphadenopathy that is a hallmark of the early stage of the disease.

 

 

  • Cause: Sleeping sickness is caused by Trypanosoma brucei, a hemoflagellate parasite transmitted by the tsetse fly (Glossina).
  • Infective Form: The infective form is the trypomastigote, found in the saliva of the tsetse fly.
  • Pathogenesis: After the tsetse fly bites, the trypomastigotes enter the human bloodstream. Early in the disease, the infection causes lymphadenopathy, specifically in the posterior cervical region, which is termed Winterbottom sign.
  • Clinical Course: The disease progresses in two stages:
  1. Hemolymphatic Stage: Characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom sign), and systemic symptoms.
  2. Neurological Stage: Involves CNS invasion, leading to altered sleep patterns, coma, and death if untreated.

 

Additional Information on Trypanosoma cruzi

 

Trypanosoma cruzi is another species of hemoflagellate parasite that causes Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis), which is distinct from African sleeping sickness. Key features of T. cruzi include:

 

  • Geographical Location: Found predominantly in Central and South America.
  • Vector: The parasite is transmitted by the feces of the reduviid bug (kissing bug) during a bite.
  • Infective Form: The infective form is also the trypomastigote, similar to T. brucei.
  • Pathogenesis: After infection, the trypomastigotes invade host cells and transform into amastigotes, which replicate and lead to cell damage. Chronic infection can result in cardiomyopathy, megaesophagus, and megacolon.
  • Key Signs: Romana’s sign (unilateral periorbital swelling) is a hallmark of acute T. cruzi infection.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Unilateral conjunctivitis: Incorrect. Unilateral conjunctivitis is not associated with Winterbottom sign or African trypanosomiasis. Instead, conjunctivitis may occur in other infections like Chlamydia trachomatis or viral conjunctivitis.

 

Option C. Narcolepsy: Incorrect. Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and is unrelated to African trypanosomiasis.

 

Option D. Transient erythema: Incorrect. Transient erythema is not a hallmark of African trypanosomiasis. Skin erythema may occur as part of other conditions such as allergic reactions or infections.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Winterbottom sign refers to posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, which is a classic feature of early-stage African trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei and transmitted by the tsetse fly (Glossina).

questions.stem: Which among the following exist in yeast form at 37°C and hyphal form at 25°C?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Histoplasma capsulatum 

 

The question is asking about dimorphic fungi, which can exist in two different forms based on the temperature:

 

  • Yeast form at 37°C: Spherical and divide by budding.
  • Mould form at 25°C: Branching hyphae with or without septa.

 

Histoplasma capsulatum is a classic example of a dimorphic fungus. At body temperature (37°C), it exists as a yeast, and at environmental temperatures (25°C), it transitions to a mould form.

 

Categorization of fungi based on morphology:

 

  1. Yeasts: Spherical, divide by budding (e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans).
  2. Moulds: Branching hyphae, can be septate or aseptate (e.g., Aspergillus, dermatophytes).
  3. Dimorphic fungi: Exist as yeast at 37°C and mould at 25°C (e.g., Histoplasma capsulatum).
  4. Yeast-like fungi: Yeast forms with pseudo-hyphae (e.g., Candida species).

 

Histoplasma capsulatum fits into the dimorphic category, as it exhibits yeast and hyphal forms based on temperature.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Malassezia furfur: Incorrect because it is a yeast-like fungus, not dimorphic.

 

Option B. Cryptococcus neoformans: Incorrect because it exists solely as a yeast and does not transition to a mould form.

 

Option C. Aspergillus: Incorrect because it is a mould and does not exhibit yeast-like characteristics.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dimorphic fungi, such as Histoplasma capsulatum, exist as yeast at 37°C and mould at 25°C.

questions.stem: Infective form to mosquito in plasmodium falciparum:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Gametocytes

 

The infective form for the mosquito in the life cycle of Plasmodium falciparum is the gametocyte.

 

 Here is how the process works:

 

  1. Human Stage: When a mosquito takes a blood meal from an infected human, it ingests male and female gametocytes present in the human blood.
  2. In the Mosquito: Inside the mosquito’s gut, the male and female gametocytes fuse to form a zygote. The zygote develops into an ookinete, which penetrates the mosquito’s gut wall to form an oocyst. Sporozoites are then produced in the oocyst.
  3. Completion: The sporozoites migrate to the salivary glands of the mosquito. When the mosquito bites another human, it transmits the sporozoites, which are the infective form for humans.

 

Thus, while the infective form for humans is the sporozoite, the infective form for the mosquito is the gametocyte.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Merozoites: Incorrect. Merozoites are formed in the liver and bloodstream of humans but do not play a role in infecting mosquitoes.

 

Option B. Sporozoites: Incorrect. Sporozoites are the infective form for humans, not mosquitoes.

 

Option D. Trophozoites: Incorrect. Trophozoites are the active feeding stage of Plasmodium in humans and do not infect mosquitoes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The infective form of Plasmodium falciparum for mosquitoes is the gametocyte, while the infective form for humans is the sporozoite. Importantly, the mosquito (female Anopheles) is the definitive host as sexual reproduction of the parasite occurs in the mosquito.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the vector that is involved in following diagnostic image:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ixodid tick 

 

The diagnostic image provided reveals intraerythrocytic parasites forming a characteristic Maltese cross, which is a hallmark feature of Babesia infection.

 

Key features visible in the image:

 

  • The red blood cells (RBCs) are infected.
  • The intraerythrocytic parasite forms a cross-shaped pattern, which is unique to Babesia.

 

Babesia is a protozoan parasite that infects RBCs and is transmitted by Ixodid ticks (hard ticks), specifically the genus Ixodes. This condition is referred to as babesiosis and often mimics malaria in clinical presentation, with symptoms including fever, chills, hemolytic anemia, and fatigue. Unlike Plasmodium, Babesia does not form pigment granules.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Female anopheles mosquito: Incorrect. Female Anopheles mosquitoes are vectors for Plasmodium species, which cause malaria. They are not involved in the transmission of Babesia.

 

Option C. Glossina: Incorrect. The Glossina fly, also known as the tsetse fly, is the vector for Trypanosoma brucei, which causes African sleeping sickness. It does not transmit Babesia.

 

Option D. Reduviid bug: Incorrect. The Reduviid bug, or "kissing bug," transmits Trypanosoma cruzi, the causative agent of Chagas disease. It is not involved in the transmission of Babesia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The vector for Babesia is the Ixodid tick, specifically species from the Ixodes genus. The hallmark diagnostic feature is the presence of the Maltese cross within RBCs, visible under microscopy.
